# PART 1 – The repository {#part-1-the-repository .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1
:::

::: notes
Part one turns the folder of your workspace into a git repository. Until now the workspace has been a plain folder, deliberately, so that nobody had to learn git in the middle of the workshop. Git records the history of a folder as a sequence of deliberate snapshots, each with a date, an author and a sentence saying why it was taken. In this case the repository also has to keep out what the licence of GESIS forbids sharing. The first snapshot that it records will be your preregistration, as you declared it, before a word of the report is written.
:::

## Git in Positron {#git-in-positron .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**The Source Control view** (Ctrl+Shift+G) holds the three places of git:

- **Changes** – the working directory, every file whose changes are not yet staged
- **Staged Changes** – the staging area, the changes gathered for the next commit
- **Graph** – the repository, one commit to a line, newest first
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**The loop**, one change at a time:

1. Edit a file and save it
2. Stage it with the plus sign on its row, or every file with the plus sign on the header of Changes
3. Write a message in the box above the lists, saying what the change does
4. Press Commit, or Ctrl+Enter in the box
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Once on each machine, in a terminal (**Terminal → New Terminal**), git needs your name and email address for every commit: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"`.
:::

::: {.src}
Git and GitHub for reproducible research, section 2, on the AR4DS site: codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html
:::

::: notes
Positron does the work of git in its Source Control view, which opens from the Activity Bar or with control shift G. The view holds the three places that git keeps. Changes is your working directory: every file that you have changed and not yet staged. Staged Changes is the holding area for the next snapshot. And the Graph at the foot of the view is the repository itself, one commit to a line. The loop is always the same: edit and save, stage what belongs together with the plus sign, write a message that says what the change does, and commit. The letter beside each file says what happened to it: U for a file that git does not track yet, A for added, M for modified. [advance] Git stamps every commit with a name and an email address, so set them once on each machine, in a terminal.
:::

## What stays out of the repository {#what-stays-out-of-the-repository .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The `.gitignore` of the workspace already names what git must not track: `/data_private/`, which holds the respondent file and everything built from it; `/_site/` and `/.quarto/`, the rendered report and the working files of Quarto; and `.class-tag`, your tag on the class chart
- In Positron the Explorer shows each ignored file in a paler grey, and the list of changes in the Source Control view leaves such files out
- The waves from GESIS belong in a folder outside the workspace, where the build script looks for them. As a backstop, the `.gitignore` also refuses `.dta`, `.sav` and `.por` files, zip archives and R data files anywhere in the folder
- The report works on the aggregate files in `data/`. A chunk that read the respondent file would write its output into `_freeze/`, which git tracks
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A file that is committed and pushed stays in the history of the repository even after it is deleted. Read the list under **Changes** before the first commit: nothing from `data_private/` and no `.dta` file may appear in it.
:::

::: {.src}
The `.gitignore` and the README of the workspace; Git and GitHub for reproducible research, section 4.
:::

::: notes
Before the first commit, decide what the repository must never hold, because its history is permanent. The workspace has done most of that for you. Its gitignore file names the private folder, which holds the respondent file that you built after the second day and everything built from it, then the rendered site and the working files of Quarto, and your tag for the class chart. Positron shows such files in a paler grey and leaves them out of the list of changes. As a backstop, the gitignore file also refuses the formats in which GESIS distributes the waves, zip archives and R data files, wherever in the folder such files are saved, although the waves themselves belong outside the workspace, where the build script looks for them. One gap remains, and closing it is up to you. The report should stay on the aggregate files, because the frozen results of every chunk are tracked, and a chunk that read the respondent file would carry its output into the repository. [advance] So read the list under Changes before you commit.
:::

## Hands-on 1 – The first commit {#hands-on-1-the-first-commit .smaller}

::: {.small}
1. Open the folder of your workspace, `replication-lab-main`, with **File → Open Folder…**, and check the preregistration block of Task 5, the chunk labelled `prereg` in `index.qmd`: one choice on each `my_` line, and fields 1 and 4 completed. If you declared in the browser lab, copy the block from your notes first, exactly as you declared it
2. Once on this machine, set your name and email address with `git config --global`
3. In Source Control, press **Initialize Repository**. The files of the workspace appear under Changes, marked U: read the list, and check that it holds no `.dta` file and nothing from `data_private/`
4. Stage all the changes with **Stage All Changes**, the plus sign on the header of Changes, write a message such as `Add the workspace with the analysis declared in Task 5`, and commit
5. Hold the pointer over the commit in the Graph: its author, its date and time, and the short form of its identifier
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This commit is the declaration. Everything that you write from now on comes after it in the history.
:::

::: notes
Your turn. Open the folder of your workspace, the one that you used yesterday, and look at the preregistration block of Task 5 before you do anything else: every my line should hold your choice, and the two dotted lines, the claim in your own words and the sentence from your causal graph, should be filled in. If they are not, fill them in now, from your notes of yesterday, and only then go on. If you declared in the browser lab, copy the block that you saved in your notes into the report first, exactly as you declared it. Set your name and email address in a terminal if this machine has never had them. Then press Initialize Repository, read the list of changes for anything from GESIS, stage everything, and commit with a message that says what the commit holds. [state the time] [advance] That commit is your declaration, and everything that follows this afternoon will sit after it in the history.
:::

# PART 2 – The report {#part-2-the-report .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2
:::

::: notes
Part two is the report itself. It is short: one section, in four parts, written around the analysis that you declared. What makes it a report rather than a page of notes is that every number in it is computed when it renders, from the same run as the output beside it, so that the text cannot fall out of step with the analysis. I show you what the four parts are and how to compute the numbers, and then you write.
:::

## What the report contains {#what-the-report-contains .smaller}

::: {.small}
A section of its own, between the paragraph **A second declared specification?** and the box *Taking it home*, in this order:

1. **The result with its uncertainty**, under the errors that you declared: the slope, its conventional t on its df, and the CR2 p on its Satterthwaite df, as `run_spec()` prints them
2. **Its place on the curve of the claim**: the share of the 864 specifications on the curve whose claim-aligned r is more negative, from the placement line of the printout
3. **Any departure from the declaration**, and the reason for it, or a sentence saying that there was none
4. **What the replication with new data adds**: SCORE replicated the claim on fourteen Standard waves fielded between 2013 and 2019, and found a positive coefficient for unemployment, not significant, so the replication was not successful by the criterion of SCORE
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The claim comes from the paper [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] as SCORE selected it for Multi100 [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], and the reference list at the end of the report already holds both.
:::

::: {.src}
The SCORE dossier of the paper, osf.io/h7432; the replication as Part 4 of the one-day workshop presents it.
:::

::: notes
Here is what goes into the report, and in this order. First the result with its uncertainty, under the errors that you declared: the slope, its t, and the CR2 p-value on its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, exactly as the helper of Task 5 prints them. Second, its place on the curve of the claim, the share of the specifications whose claim-aligned correlation is more negative than yours. Third, any departure from your declaration, with the reason, or a plain sentence that there was none, because a departure reported with its reason is part of a good report, and a hidden one is not. Fourth, what the replication adds. The new waves gave a positive coefficient, not significant. Your result says what the original panel supports under your choices, the replication what happened when the question was put to later surveys, and the report needs both.
:::

## Numbers in the report {#numbers-in-the-report .smaller}

::: {.small}
- In the chunk `run-spec`, keep what the helper returns: `result <- run_spec(my_model)` prints the same lines and stores every number of the printout
- In the text, inline code computes each number when the report renders, and `sprintf()` sets its decimals, as the report itself does elsewhere
:::

::: {.fs-75}
```{.markdown}
## The declared analysis

The declared specification gives a slope of `r sprintf("%.5f", result$b)`, with t = `r sprintf("%.2f", result$t)`
on `r result$df` degrees of freedom under conventional errors, and a CR2 p of `r sprintf("%.4f", result$p_cr2)`
on `r sprintf("%.1f", result$df_cr2)` Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
```
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
`result` also holds `placement`, the share of the specifications on the curve with a more negative claim-aligned r, the claim-aligned r itself, `r_ca`, and the country-years analysed, `n`. For GDP growth the printout flips the signs of b and t, while `result$b` and `result$t` keep the signs of the fit. The header sets `date: today`, so every render carries its own date.
:::

::: notes
The numbers come from your run of the declared specification. In the chunk labelled run-spec, write result, arrow, in front of the call. The helper prints exactly what it printed yesterday, and it also hands back every number of its printout, so you can keep them. In the text, inline code does the rest: a backtick, the letter r, and an expression, and when the report renders, the expression is replaced by its value. Use sprintf for the decimals, as the report does elsewhere, because the setup chunk of the report tells R to print four digits, and an inline slope would come out rounded to four decimal places. [advance] Result holds more than the slide uses: the placement, the claim-aligned correlation and the count of country-years. If you declared growth, mind the signs: the printout flips them for the claim, and the stored slope keeps the sign of the fit.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – Writing the report {#hands-on-2-writing-the-report .smaller}

::: {.small}
1. Line 3 of `index.qmd`, `author: "Pair: [names]"`: put your own name, save, and commit with a message such as `Name the author of the report`
2. In the chunk `run-spec`, write `result <- run_spec(my_model)`
3. Between the paragraph **A second declared specification?** and the box *Taking it home*, add `## The declared analysis` and write the first part, with its numbers as inline code. Render, read it, and commit
4. Write the other three parts, and render and commit after each of them, with a message that says what the commit adds
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your IDE previews the report with Ctrl+Shift+K. An inline expression that fails stops the render, with a message to read from the top.
:::

::: notes
Your turn, and this is the longest stretch of the afternoon. Start with the smallest change, your own name in the header, and commit it, so that the loop of part one becomes a habit. Then keep the result of the helper in the chunk run-spec. Then the section: a heading after the paragraph about a second declared specification, and the first part, the result with its test, with every number as inline code. Render it, read it as a reader would, and commit. Then the other three parts, each followed by a render and a commit with a message that says what it adds. [advance] If a render fails, read the message from the top, where the first lines say where it stopped, and I will come round. [state the time]
:::

# PART 3 – The record {#part-3-the-record .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 3
:::

::: notes
Part three makes the report into a record that someone else can trust. Two habits do most of the work. A render from a clean session shows that the report makes everything that it uses, so that it would run on anyone's machine. And a history of small commits, each with a message that says what changed, shows how the analysis reached its final form, including any step away from what you declared. Publishing the report on the web comes at the end, for those who want it.
:::

## A render from a clean session {#a-render-from-a-clean-session .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Quarto renders in a fresh R process of its own. An object that only the console made is missing there, and the render stops at the first chunk that needs it
- Restart R with **Interpreter: Restart Active Interpreter Session** (Ctrl+Shift+0), then type `quarto render` in a terminal. It renders the codebooks in `data/` and the report, and ends with `Output created: _site\index.html`
- When a render fails, the line that begins `Quitting from` names the lines of the chunk and its label, such as `[run-spec]`
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Three things break a clean render: an object made in the console and never in the report, a file read from a path that exists only on your machine, and a package attached in your session but not named in the code. Each would break the report for anyone else as well.
:::

::: {.src}
Quarto documents, sections 3 and 11, on the AR4DS site: codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/quarto.html
:::

::: notes
The objects in your console exist only in your session, and a render never uses them. Quarto starts a fresh R process for every render, runs every chunk from the top and throws the process away at the end, so a report that renders is a report whose chunks make everything that it uses. The test is cheap: restart R, so that the Variables pane empties, and render from a terminal. In this workspace the render takes the three codebooks in the data folder along with the report, so do not be surprised by four files in the log. If it fails, the message tells you where: the line that begins Quitting from gives the lines of the chunk and its label. [advance] In practice, almost every failure comes from one of three things: something made in the console and never in the report, a path that exists only on your machine, or a package that your session had loaded but your code never names.
:::

## A history of the analysis {#a-history-of-the-analysis .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **One change, one commit**, with a message that says what the change does, as if completing "this commit will…": `Leave out the respondents who mentioned no frame`
- Two changes in one file can still be two commits: in the diff editor, the plus sign beside a change, **Stage Block**, stages that change alone
- A change to the preregistration block after the first commit is a **departure from the declaration**, and the Graph records it with its date: say so in part 3 of the report
- The **Timeline**, at the foot of the Explorer, lists the commits that changed the file open in the editor
:::

::: {.src}
Git and GitHub for reproducible research, sections 2 and 5, on the AR4DS site: codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html
:::

::: notes
A history is only as useful as its messages. A commit should hold one change, and its message should say what the change does, written as if it completed the sentence: this commit will. The example on the slide is one decision of the menu, and its message names it. When two changes end up in one file, the diff editor can stage one of them on its own, so that each commit still records one thing. Notice what the history does for your declaration. Your first commit holds the preregistration block as you declared it. If you change that block later, for any reason, the change is a commit with a date, and anyone can read it, and part three of your report is the place to say what changed and why. The Timeline gives you the history of one file at a glance.
:::

## Hands-on 3 – The clean render and the history {#hands-on-3-the-clean-render-and-the-history .smaller}

::: {.small}
1. Restart R (Ctrl+Shift+0), and check that the Variables pane is empty
2. In a terminal, type `quarto render`. Then preview with Ctrl+Shift+K, and check every number of your section against the last render
3. Fix whatever breaks, and commit the fix with a message that says what was wrong
4. With `index.qmd` open, unfold the **Timeline** at the foot of the Explorer, and read your history from the declaration to the last part of the report
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Swap with a neighbour: could they say, from your history alone, what you declared, what you found and whether you departed from the declaration?
:::

::: notes
Your turn. Restart R and check that the Variables pane is empty. Render from a terminal, then preview, and compare every number of your section with the last render. If something breaks, it is almost always one of the three causes on the slide about the clean render: fix it in the report, not in the console, render again, and commit the fix with a message that says what was wrong. Then open the Timeline of the report and read your own history from the top. [state the time] [advance] Last, swap with a neighbour and read each other's histories. Could your neighbour say, from the messages alone, what you declared, what you found and whether you departed from your declaration? If not, write fuller messages from now on.
:::

## Publishing the report {#publishing-the-report .smaller .deepdive run="publish"}

::: {.small}
- With every change committed and no remote, the Source Control view offers **Publish Branch**. It asks to sign in to GitHub, so that Positron can create the repository there, and pushes your history to it
- On GitHub, **Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions**. From then on every push to `main` runs the workflow of the workspace, `.github/workflows/publish.yml`, which installs R and the packages, renders the report again and publishes it at `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repository>/`
- After each new commit, **Sync Changes** pushes it, and the published report follows
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A published report is public. The derived country-year data in `data/` are released under CC BY 4.0, as the `LICENSE` of the workspace states, while the Eurobarometer microdata stay under the terms of GESIS and never enter a repository.
:::

::: {.src}
The workflow, the README and the LICENSE of the workspace; Git and GitHub for reproducible research, sections 3 to 5.
:::

::: notes
Publishing is optional, and it is the step that turns your repository into something that other people can read. With everything committed, the button under the message box reads Publish Branch. It asks you to let Positron sign in to GitHub, creates the repository there and pushes your history. The workspace already carries a small workflow that renders the report on GitHub and publishes it as a web page. Switch it on once, in the settings of the repository under Pages, by choosing GitHub Actions as the source. From then on every push renders your report again, with your own results, and the page follows. [advance] Public means public in the strongest sense, so think before you publish. The country-year data of the workspace are released under an open licence, so they may go. The respondent file never may, and the gitignore keeps its folder out.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – Publishing {#hands-on-4-publishing .smaller .deepdive run="publish"}

::: {.small}
1. Commit everything, then press **Publish Branch** and sign in to GitHub when Positron asks
2. On the page of the new repository: **Settings → Pages**, and choose **GitHub Actions** as the source
3. Commit one more small change, for example a sentence in the README, and press **Sync Changes**
4. When the workflow has run, open `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repository>/` and find your section
:::

::: notes
For those who want to publish, here are the steps in order. Commit everything first, because Publish Branch appears only when nothing is waiting. Sign in to GitHub when Positron asks. On the page of your new repository, open the settings, then Pages, and choose GitHub Actions as the source. Then commit one more small change and sync it, which runs the workflow with Pages switched on. When it has finished, your report is at your own github dot io address, under the name of the repository. If the page does not appear, tell me, and we can read the log of the run together. [state the time]
:::

## After the course {#after-the-course .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Yours now**: a reproduced result, an estimand statement and a causal graph for a published claim, a declared analysis placed among the 864 specifications of its curve, and a report whose history shows the declaration before the result
- **Where to go next**: the page [After the course](../tracks/eu-frames-extended/after.html) leads into the companion curriculum, from meta-analysis and the building of the analysis file to the items behind the scales, weights, missing answers, causal graphs, simulation, and the multiverse and its critics
- **The record of the claim**: the SCORE dossier of the paper at osf.io/h7432, the maintained fork of the reanalysis behind the course panel at osf.io/6zqct, and the archival record of Multi100 at osf.io/8rtwe
- **Keep going locally**: the research-software and open-research teams at your university, or a ReproducibiliTea journal club near you
:::

::: {.fragment .none}
Everything on the course site is open, and you can fork any of it.
:::

::: notes
That is the end of the course. Three days ago we started from what a claim in social science is for and why its credibility became a question. Since then you have reproduced a recorded result to the third decimal, said precisely what question the claim answers, declared an analysis before running it, placed it among every justifiable alternative, learned the methods behind those alternatives at the level of the country-year and of the respondent, and written it up in a report whose history anyone can check. The page After the course, on the site, leads into the modules that three days could only touch, and the OSF holds the record of the claim, from the SCORE dossier to the archive of Multi100. If you want company in keeping these habits, most universities have research-software and open-research teams, and ReproducibiliTea journal clubs meet in many places. [advance] And everything on the course site is open: take any of it and make it your own.
:::

  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current

  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }

        }

      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
